title: For Us, There's Only War
author: Juan
summary: Writing under the newsletter Simple Men, the author Juan articulates a generational theory of masculine duty framed as spiritual and cultural warfare. He opens by naming and rejecting his own escapist fantasy, a quiet life with wife, children, and land, arguing that retreat from a 'toxic' culture would abandon other suffering men and is therefore both naive and cowardly given the scale of what he sees as civilizational decline. The essay's structuring claim is that the present generation of men is called to sacrifice personal peace for a fight whose fruits, a freer, more honorable world, will only be enjoyed by descendants, not by the men fighting now. Framed explicitly in religious terms (invoking God, sacrifice, and judgment before Heaven), the piece belongs to the broader manosphere and men's-formation genre: it diagnoses widespread male numbness and pain (hidden behind 'sad smiles' and alcohol), names technology and 'this technocratic monstrosity' as part of what must be resisted, and casts fatherhood's ultimate purpose as securing a future for children the author himself may never see realized.
points: The essay's core argument is a deliberate rejection of a passive, retreat-oriented model of masculinity ('my dream is naive and cowardly') in favor of an active, sacrificial one, framing withdrawal from cultural conflict as itself a moral failure.

It explicitly frames the current generation of men as instrumental rather than beneficiary: the described sacrifice ('fifty years of disappointments... necessary sacrifice') is intended to benefit grandchildren and descendants, not the author's own generation.

The piece diagnoses a specific and observable crisis among men, describing them as hiding pain behind 'sad smiles' and numbing themselves with alcohol, and treats that observation as part of its justification for calling men to purposeful struggle rather than resignation.

Technology and surveillance culture ('this technocratic monstrosity that we've built tracking their every thought') are named as part of what the imagined future freedom must be freed from, tying the essay's masculinity framework to a broader critique of modern tech-mediated life.

The essay grounds its call to sacrifice explicitly in religious accountability, framing the ultimate validation of a man's struggle as standing 'before God' rather than in any earthly outcome or recognition.
quotes: I also dream of something simpler: my wife, my children, some animals, and a peaceful life in the mountains, away from the chaos and toxicity of our times.

And as much as it pains me to accept it, my dream is naive and cowardly, for to live it would be to abandon the fight and run away into hiding, leaving behind all those souls who are lost and hurting.

We are the weak men amidst the hard times. And it will stay that way until someone has the guts to lead the charge and bring about the next phase of this never-ending cycle. Someone has to do it. Might as well be us.

I accept the possibility that I won't get to see the end of this war. All I can hope for is that before my death comes, I will have done some good, and I will have fought bravely and honorably, for a cause greater than my own selfish goals and dreams.

For us, there might be only war. Fifty years of disappointments, fifty years of pain, fifty years of necessary sacrifice to expose the horrors that lurk beneath the surface of this putrid and corrupted social fabric.
But not us. Not now. Not here. Not today. Our duty is to fight. If we are to give our children the freedom we strive for, we can't cowardly retreat and abandon the fight.
